```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr); library(ggplot2); library(stringr)
```

> **How to use this file.** Set `data_file` below to the name of the exam dataset (CSV or Excel).
> The column names are assumed from the exam paper: `bact_isolated, site, year, age, Var1-Var5, Sex,
> Education, BoiledWater`. If your names differ, change them in the **rename** step only.
> If the file is not found, the document builds **simulated demo data** so you can test the code.
> Replace the simulated results with your own when you have the real file.

# 1. Import the dataset into R

```{r import}
data_file <- "pathogen.csv"     # <- change to your file name (.csv or .xlsx)

if (file.exists(data_file)) {
  df <- if (grepl("\\.xlsx?$", data_file)) readxl::read_excel(data_file) else read_csv(data_file)
  using_demo <- FALSE
} else {
  set.seed(123); n <- 600
  df <- tibble(
    bact_isolated = sample(c("E. coli", "Salmonella", "Shigella", "Vibrio cholerae", "Klebsiella"),
                           n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.35, .2, .15, .1, .2)),
    site  = sample(c("Kigali", "Huye", "Musanze", "Rubavu"), n, replace = TRUE),
    year  = sample(2010:2020, n, replace = TRUE),
    age   = round(pmax(0, rnorm(n, 25, 18))),
    Var2  = rnorm(n, 50, 10), Var3 = rnorm(n, 20, 5), Var4 = rnorm(n, 5, 2), Var5 = rnorm(n, 100, 15),
    Sex   = sample(c("Male", "Female", "M", "female", NA), n, replace = TRUE),
    Education = sample(c("None", "Primary", "Secondary", "University"), n, replace = TRUE),
    BoiledWater = sample(c("Yes", "No"), n, replace = TRUE)
  )
  df$Var1 <- 10 + 0.3 * df$age + 0.5 * df$Var2 + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
  df <- bind_rows(df, df[1:5, ])                     # add duplicates for the cleaning demo
  using_demo <- TRUE
}
if (using_demo) cat("NOTE: simulated demo data are being used.\n")

# Harmonise names here if your file uses different ones, e.g. rename(Age = age_years)
names(df)[tolower(names(df)) == "age"] <- "Age"
names(df)[tolower(names(df)) == "sex"] <- "Sex"
head(df)
```

# 2. How many variables and observations?

```{r dims}
dim(df)
cat("Observations (rows):", nrow(df), "\nVariables (columns):", ncol(df), "\n")
str(df)
```

# 3. Clean the dataset

```{r clean}
colSums(is.na(df))                 # missing values
sum(duplicated(df))                # duplicates

df <- df %>%
  distinct() %>%                                                    # remove duplicates
  mutate(across(where(is.character), str_squish)) %>%               # remove extra spaces
  mutate(Sex = case_when(str_to_lower(Sex) %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
                         str_to_lower(Sex) %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female",
                         TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%                 # harmonise Sex
  filter(!is.na(bact_isolated), !is.na(Age), Age >= 0, Age <= 110)  # drop impossible / missing key values

dim(df)
```

# 4. Prevalence of `bact_isolated` (bar chart)

```{r prev}
prev <- df %>% count(bact_isolated) %>% mutate(prevalence = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
prev
ggplot(prev, aes(reorder(bact_isolated, -prevalence), prevalence, fill = bact_isolated)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) + geom_text(aes(label = paste0(prevalence, "%")), vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(title = "Prevalence of isolated bacteria", x = "Bacteria isolated", y = "Prevalence (%)")
```

# 5. Side-by-side bar chart: distribution of `bact_isolated` by site

```{r site}
ggplot(df, aes(site, fill = bact_isolated)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Bacteria isolated by site", x = "Site", y = "Number of isolates", fill = "Bacteria")
```

# 6. Trend from 2014 for each bacteria (one graph)

```{r trend}
df %>% filter(year >= 2014) %>% count(year, bact_isolated) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, n, colour = bact_isolated)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Trend of each bacteria since 2014", x = "Year", y = "Number of isolates", colour = "Bacteria")
```

# 7. Young (under 16) versus adults (above 16)

Outliers in age are removed **once**, before splitting, so the **same observations** are used for both
groups and in every later analysis.

```{r groups}
q   <- quantile(df$Age, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE); iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
df_nout <- df %>% filter(Age >= q[1] - 1.5 * iqr, Age <= q[2] + 1.5 * iqr)
cat("Removed outliers:", nrow(df) - nrow(df_nout), "\n")

young  <- df_nout %>% filter(Age < 16)
adults <- df_nout %>% filter(Age >= 16)
cat("Young:", nrow(young), "| Adults:", nrow(adults), "| Total:", nrow(df_nout), "\n")
stopifnot(nrow(young) + nrow(adults) == nrow(df_nout))     # nobody lost

comp <- bind_rows(mutate(young, group = "Young (<16)"), mutate(adults, group = "Adults (>=16)")) %>%
  count(group, bact_isolated) %>% group_by(group) %>% mutate(prevalence = n / sum(n) * 100) %>% ungroup()
comp

ggplot(comp, aes(bact_isolated, prevalence, fill = group)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Bacteria prevalence: young vs adults", x = "Bacteria", y = "Prevalence (%)", fill = NULL)

# Is the difference significant?
chisq.test(table(bind_rows(mutate(young, g = "Young"), mutate(adults, g = "Adult"))[, c("g", "bact_isolated")]))
```

# 8. Model building

All models use `df_nout` (same observations as step 7).

## I. Multiple linear regression (Var1 ~ Age + Var2-Var5 + Sex + Education + BoiledWater)

```{r m1}
m1 <- lm(Var1 ~ Age + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + Sex + Education + BoiledWater, data = df_nout)
summary(m1)
```

## II. Simple linear regression with Age only

```{r m2}
m2 <- lm(Var1 ~ Age, data = df_nout)
summary(m2)
```

## III. Statistical significance of Age

```{r sig}
coef(summary(m2))["Age", ]
confint(m2)["Age", ]
```
If the p-value for `Age` is **below 0.05**, Age is significantly associated with Var1. The slope tells
how much Var1 changes for each extra year of age.

## IV. Scatter plot with fitted line

```{r scatter}
ggplot(df_nout, aes(Age, Var1)) + geom_point(alpha = .5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Var1 versus Age", x = "Age (years)", y = "Var1")
```
**Patterns to describe:** direction (upward = positive relationship), strength (tight cloud = strong),
shape (curve = not linear) and outliers.

## V. Model assumptions (diagnostic plots)

```{r diag, fig.height = 7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(m2); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
shapiro.test(residuals(m2)[1:min(5000, length(residuals(m2)))])   # normality of residuals
```
- **Residuals vs Fitted:** random scatter around 0 = linearity and constant variance are fine.
- **Normal Q-Q:** points on the line = residuals are normal.
- **Scale-Location:** flat line = constant variance.
- **Residuals vs Leverage:** points beyond Cook's distance lines = influential observations.

## VI. Repeat with Var2 as predictor

```{r m3}
m3 <- lm(Var1 ~ Var2, data = df_nout)
summary(m3)
```

## VII. Which model explains more variance in Var1?

```{r compare}
tibble(model = c("Var1 ~ Age", "Var1 ~ Var2"),
       R2 = c(summary(m2)$r.squared, summary(m3)$r.squared),
       adj_R2 = c(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, summary(m3)$adj.r.squared),
       p_value = c(coef(summary(m2))["Age", 4], coef(summary(m3))["Var2", 4]),
       AIC = c(AIC(m2), AIC(m3)))
```
The model with the **higher R-squared** explains more of the variance in Var1.

## VIII. Which predictor is stronger?

The stronger predictor is the one with the **higher R-squared and the smaller p-value** (and the
larger absolute t-value). Read the table above and state it in one sentence, for example:
"Var2 is the stronger predictor (R2 = ..., p < 0.001) compared with Age (R2 = ..., p = ...)."
